newsitem.title: USA: Charges hold Chrysler back from record 1996 net.
newsitem.headline: Charges hold Chrysler back from record 1996 net.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. on Tuesday said it earned net income of $807 million, or $1.12 a share, during the fourth quarter of 1996, with special charges holding the automaker back from its best full-year net profit ever.
Detroit's No. 3 automaker reported full-year 1996 net income of $3.53 billion or $4.74 per fully diluted share.
In 1995, Chrysler posted fourth quarter net income of $1.04 billion, or $1.33 a share, and full-year net income of $2.03 billion, or $2.56 a share.
Chrysler's 1996 net fell short of its 1994 record of $3.71 billion because of $347 million in special charges taken during 1996.

During the fourth quarter, Chrysler's profit was reduced by $279 million in charges that covered the early retirement of debt, higher United Auto Workers pension cost, a voluntary early retirement program and the writedown of Pentastar Electronics, a subsidiary sold to a Huntsville, Ala., investor group for $17 million.
On an operating basis, both the fourth quarter and full 1996 year were records for Chrysler.

Excluding the charges, Chrysler earned $1.09 billion in the quarter and $3.88 billion for the year, beating out its previous operating records of $1.04 billion in the fourth quarter of 1994 and $3.58 billion in the full 1994 year.
On a pre-tax basis, Chrysler also turned in its best year ever, earning $6.09 billion including charges, versus $3.45 billion in 1995.

Chrysler attributed its strong performance to a 10.7 percent increase in worldwide factory vehicle sales, to 2,958,800 from 2,673,539 in 1995. Based on strong sales of trucks, sport/utility vehicles and minivans, Chrysler's share of the U.S. and Canadian car and truck market climbed to 16.1 percent for the year from 14.7 percent in 1995.
Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton said in a statement that the company won't rest on its laurels.

"There is no end to the improvements we can achieve if we remain vigilant about controlling our costs and about continually improving our processes and our products," Eaton said. "That's the challenge we're all focused on and its one I'm confident we'll meet."

Chrysler said its employees will share the wealth, with about 79,000 U.S. hourly and salaried workers receiving an average profit sharing payment of $7,900 in February. That compares to $3,200 for the company's 1995 performance and $8,000 for the 1994 performance, which was received by about 75,200 employees.
